posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring compliance pain post with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the auditability problem with a specific observation, position explainability as the real unlock, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The 'GPT said so' answer is the whole problem in four words. It's not really a trust gap — it's an audit trail gap. Every analyst I talk to knows the insight is probably right, but if you can't walk a regulator back through the logic step by step, the number is worthless. Wonder how many BI tools are quietly facing the same scrutiny right now and just haven't hit a compliance moment yet.

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO at 140-person firm hitting the classic adoption wall — validate the trust problem specifically, add the insight that it's not a training issue
posts.draft_comment: The 18 months wasn't wasted on the wrong tool — it was wasted on the wrong problem. People don't resist dashboards because they're lazy, they resist them because they've been burned by a number that looked clean and turned out to be wrong once, in public. After that, Excel feels safer because at least they built it themselves and know where the bodies are buried. Did anyone on the finance team have a moment like that early on?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging with a post about dashboard bloat — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why' behind low adoption, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is basically the analytics equivalent of measuring everything so you're never wrong about anything. The jump from 10% to 85% usage tells the real story — people don't avoid dashboards because they're lazy, they avoid them because the dashboard doesn't reflect how they actually think about their job. The best metric isn't the most accurate one, it's the one someone will act on at 9am on a Monday. What made you pick those specific 5?

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: High-scoring post with ICP prospect (Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail) engaging — validate the 'who owns truth' framing and reframe the real failure as governance not tooling
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports problem is almost never a Power BI problem. It's a 'we skipped the hard conversation about definitions before we handed out the licenses' problem. Tooling gets the blame because it's easier to blame than the process of getting finance, ops and marketing to agree on what revenue actually means. Curious whether you think that conversation can even happen without someone being given the authority to lose a few arguments.

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO raising AI hallucinations as a material risk, with a CEO prospect engaging — validate the security framing, add the 'trust gap' layer that most analytics vendors ignore
posts.draft_comment: The framing here is exactly right and most analytics vendors are still treating this as an edge case. The real problem isn't just that the number is wrong — it's that a hallucinated output looks identical to a real one. No audit trail, no confidence signal, no way for the person reading it to know they're working with fiction. How many organisations even have a process for validating AI-generated analytics before they hit a decision-maker?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: CEO at 65-person firm naming the exact pain of BI tools built for data teams — validate with specificity, add the real reason it happens, with COO at Sterling Consulting in the thread
posts.draft_comment: That £200k number is almost a rite of passage at this size. The problem isn't usually the platform — it's that every BI tool is fundamentally designed around someone who thinks in data models, not someone who needs to know if Q3 is on track before a client call. So it gets handed off to the one person who learned it, and quietly becomes their personal spreadsheet. How many of those platforms even tested with a non-technical user before shipping?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a manufacturing/industrial firm hitting the classic 'whose numbers are right' wall — validate the cultural root cause, add the layer that culture alone isn't enough without a single definition layer underneath it.
posts.draft_comment: The filter problem is almost never a filter problem — it's that nobody agreed what 'revenue this quarter' actually means before anyone built anything. Culture helps people care about fixing it, but you still need one place where the definition lives or the same argument happens next quarter with different people in the room. Curious whether your CFO left that meeting wanting a process fix or just better tooling, because those lead to very different conversations.

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing the adoption gap in enterprise AI rollouts — validate the shadow AI insight and reframe the real problem as prompt literacy, not tool quality
posts.draft_comment: The shadow AI point is the real tell — when people are sneaking off to ChatGPT on their phones, that's not a compliance problem, it's a signal that the official tool isn't meeting them where they actually work. 12% adoption after 90 days usually means the tool answered a question nobody was actually asking. The hardest part of any analytics or AI rollout isn't access, it's teaching people what's even worth asking. Did you find the 12% who were using it — what were they doing differently?
